notes.definition: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem. A high biodiversity helps keep ecosystems stable.
explanation: Biodiversity means the variety of all the different species of organisms, either on the whole Earth or within one ecosystem. A tropical rainforest or a coral reef has very high biodiversity because it contains a huge number of different species of plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms. A field planted with a single crop such as wheat has very low biodiversity. Biodiversity is about the number of different species, not just the total number of individual organisms: a field of a million wheat plants still has low biodiversity.

A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems. In an ecosystem with many species, each species is less dependent on any one other species for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment. For example, if a predator feeds on several different prey species and one prey species declines, the predator can switch to the others. In an ecosystem with low biodiversity, the loss of one species can cause other species that depend on it to decline as well, so the whole ecosystem is more easily disrupted.

Organisms also depend on each other to maintain the physical environment. Plants hold soil together with their roots and provide shade and shelter, decomposers recycle nutrients so that plants can grow, and many plants depend on insects for pollination. When biodiversity is high, several species can often carry out each of these roles, so the loss of one species does not stop the role being carried out.

The future of the human species on Earth relies on us maintaining a good level of biodiversity. Humans depend on other species for food, for materials such as wood and fibres, and for medicines (many drugs were first discovered in plants and microorganisms). Ecosystems also provide services such as pollination of crops, clean water, fertile soil and the removal of carbon dioxide by photosynthesis. Species that have not yet been studied might provide future foods or medicines, and once a species is extinct it is lost for ever.

Many human activities are reducing biodiversity. These include using land for building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste, deforestation, pollution of water, air and land, and global warming. Only recently have measures been taken to try to stop this reduction, such as breeding programmes, protecting habitats, replanting hedgerows and reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions. These measures are covered in the subtopic on maintaining biodiversity.
keyFacts: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.
High biodiversity makes an ecosystem more stable.
It reduces the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.
The future of the human species relies on us maintaining a good level of biodiversity.
Humans rely on other species for food, materials, medicines and services such as pollination and clean water.
Many human activities are reducing biodiversity.
Only recently have measures been taken to try to stop the reduction in biodiversity.
A monoculture (a large area of one crop) has very low biodiversity.

keyTerms.definition: The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.
A group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring.
The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
The ability of an ecosystem to stay much the same over time and to recover when one part of it changes.
The way species in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.
A large area where only one type of crop is grown, giving very low biodiversity.
The permanent loss of a species: no individuals of that species remain alive anywhere.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.title: Calculating a percentage decrease in species
workedExamples.question: A survey of a pond found 25 species of invertebrate. After fertiliser ran into the pond, a repeat survey found 16 species. Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of species.

workedExamples.title: Comparing biodiversity from data
workedExamples.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. How many times more plant species were found in the woodland than in the wheat field?

workedExamples.title: Explaining stability
workedExamples.question: Explain why the population of owls in a woodland is more likely to survive a disease that kills most of the mice than owls on an island where mice are the only small mammal.
steps: In the woodland the owls also eat voles, shrews and birds, so they have other food sources.
On the island the owls depend on mice alone.
So in the high-biodiversity woodland the owls are less dependent on one species and the population is more stable.
workedExamples.answer: The woodland has higher biodiversity, so the owls can switch to other prey and are less dependent on the mice.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think biodiversity means the number of organisms in an area.
misconceptions.right: In fact, biodiversity means the variety of different species. A huge field of one crop has many organisms but low biodiversity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think biodiversity only matters for wildlife and not for people.
misconceptions.right: In fact, humans depend on biodiversity for food, materials, medicines, pollination of crops and clean water, so the future of the human species relies on it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think losing one species from an ecosystem only affects that species.
misconceptions.right: In fact, other species that depend on it for food, shelter or pollination can also decline, especially in ecosystems with low biodiversity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think humans have always tried to protect biodiversity.
misconceptions.right: In fact, the AQA specification states that only recently have measures been taken to try to stop the reduction in biodiversity.

realWorld: Many medicines come from living organisms: aspirin was developed from a chemical found in willow bark and penicillin from a mould.
About three quarters of the world's main food crops benefit from animal pollination, so the loss of pollinating insects threatens food production.
Tropical rainforests cover a small part of the Earth's land surface but contain a large proportion of all known species, so deforestation has a big effect on global biodiversity.
Coral reefs have very high biodiversity and support fisheries that feed millions of people.
examTips: Learn the definition word for word: the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.
When explaining why biodiversity matters, use the phrase 'reduces the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment'.
Do not confuse biodiversity with population size: always talk about the number of different species.
In data questions, quote numbers from the table or graph and calculate percentage changes using the original value.
Give specific human benefits (food, medicines, materials, pollination) rather than just saying biodiversity is 'good for us'.
summary: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species on Earth or in an ecosystem.
High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable.
It reduces dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the physical environment.
Humans rely on biodiversity for food, materials, medicines and ecosystem services.
Many human activities are reducing biodiversity.
Only recently have measures been taken to try to stop the reduction.

flashcards.back: It reduces the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.

flashcards.front: Why does the future of humans depend on biodiversity?

flashcards.front: Name three human activities that reduce biodiversity.

No. Only recently have measures been taken to try to stop its reduction.

flashcards.front: Which has higher biodiversity: a rainforest or a wheat field?
flashcards.back: A rainforest, because it contains many more different species.
A large area growing only one type of crop, which has low biodiversity.

flashcards.front: Give an example of a medicine that came from an organism.
flashcards.back: Aspirin (from willow bark) or penicillin (from a mould).
Species in a community depending on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.

flashcards.front: Is biodiversity the same as population size?
flashcards.back: No. Biodiversity is about the number of different species, not the number of individuals.

flashcards.front: Give one way organisms maintain the physical environment for others.
flashcards.back: For example roots hold soil together, trees give shade and shelter, decomposers recycle nutrients.

flashcards.front: What happens to a predator in a low-biodiversity ecosystem if its only prey dies out?
flashcards.back: It has no alternative food, so its population falls sharply or dies out.

questions.question: What is biodiversity?
options: The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem
The total number of organisms in an ecosystem
The number of plants in a habitat
The mass of living material in a food chain
markScheme: 1 mark: the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is about the variety of species. The total number of organisms is not the same thing, and the mass of living material is biomass.

questions.question: Which habitat is likely to have the highest biodiversity?
options: A field of barley
A garden lawn
A tropical rainforest
A car park
markScheme: 1 mark: a tropical rainforest
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests contain a huge number of different species. A barley field is a monoculture and a lawn is mostly a few grass species.

questions.question: Which human activity reduces biodiversity?
options: Clearing a forest to build houses
Planting hedgerows around fields
Setting up a nature reserve
Running a breeding programme for an endangered species
markScheme: 1 mark: clearing a forest to build houses
questions.explanation: Clearing forest destroys habitat and removes many species. The other three are measures to maintain biodiversity.

questions.question: A field contains one million wheat plants and very few other species. Which statement is correct?
options: The field has high biodiversity because there are so many plants
The field has no biodiversity at all
Biodiversity cannot be judged for a field
The field has low biodiversity because there are very few different species
markScheme: 1 mark: low biodiversity because there are very few different species
questions.explanation: Biodiversity depends on the number of different species, not the number of individuals. The field has some biodiversity (wheat and a few other species), so 'none' is wrong.

questions.question: Why does high biodiversity help to keep an ecosystem stable?
options: It reduces the dependence of one species on another for food and shelter
It means every species has more offspring
It stops all predators from feeding
It keeps the temperature of the ecosystem constant
markScheme: 1 mark: it reduces the dependence of one species on another for food and shelter
questions.explanation: With many species, each organism usually has several food sources and places to shelter, so losing one species has less effect on others.

questions.question: Which of these is a benefit that humans get directly from biodiversity?
options: Fossil fuels formed millions of years ago
Medicines developed from chemicals found in plants
Sunlight
Minerals mined from rocks
markScheme: 1 mark: medicines developed from chemicals found in plants
questions.explanation: Many medicines come from living organisms. Sunlight and minerals are non-living, and fossil fuels come from organisms that died millions of years ago, not from present-day biodiversity.

questions.question: In an ecosystem a species of bee is the only pollinator of a particular flower. What is most likely to happen to the flower if the bee dies out?
options: The flower population increases because it has less competition
The flower population is not affected
The flower population falls because it cannot be pollinated to make seeds
The flower changes its colour to attract birds
markScheme: 1 mark: the flower population falls because it cannot be pollinated
questions.explanation: The flower depends on the bee for pollination, so without it the flower cannot make seeds. Organisms cannot change their features in response to need.

questions.question: Which statement about biodiversity is correct according to the AQA specification?
options: Humans have protected biodiversity for hundreds of years
Measures to try to stop the reduction in biodiversity have only been taken recently
Biodiversity is increasing worldwide because of human activity
Human activities have no effect on biodiversity
markScheme: 1 mark: measures have only been taken recently
questions.explanation: Many human activities are reducing biodiversity, and only recently have measures been taken to try to stop this.

questions.question: Two ecosystems each lose one species of herbivore. Ecosystem P has 12 herbivore species; ecosystem Q has 2. Which statement best explains which ecosystem will be affected more?
options: Q, because predators in Q are more dependent on the remaining herbivore
P, because more species compete for food
Both are affected equally because one species is lost from each
P, because it has a larger total population
markScheme: 1 mark: Q, because predators depend more on fewer prey species
questions.explanation: In Q, losing one of two herbivores halves the prey species available to predators, so the effect on the food web is much bigger than in P.

questions.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. Which habitat has the second highest number of plant species?
options: Woodland
Lawn
Wheat field
Meadow
markScheme: 1 mark: meadow
questions.explanation: Woodland has 42 species, meadow 32, lawn 12 and wheat field 2, so the meadow is second highest.

questions.question: Use the bar chart in the notes. How many more plant species were found in the meadow than on the lawn?
questions.explanation: The meadow has 32 species and the lawn 12, so the difference is 20 species.

questions.question: A survey found 40 species of bird in an area of forest. After part of the forest was cleared, a second survey found 26 species. Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of bird species.
questions.explanation: The decrease is 14 species. 14 ÷ 40 = 0.35, which is a 35% decrease. Dividing by 26 instead gives the wrong answer.

questions.question: A hedgerow survey found 15 species of insect. Five years after the farmer stopped spraying insecticide, 24 species were found. Calculate the percentage increase.
questions.explanation: The increase is 9 species, and 9 ÷ 15 × 100 = 60%.

questions.question: A country had 250 known species of amphibian. Scientists report that 22% of them are threatened with extinction. Calculate how many species are not threatened.
markScheme: 1 mark: 22% of 250 = 55 species threatened
1 mark: 250 − 55 = 195 species not threatened
questions.explanation: 0.22 × 250 = 55 threatened species. 250 − 55 = 195. You could also calculate 0.78 × 250 = 195.

questions.question: A coral reef contained 320 species of fish. After a period of coral damage, the number of fish species fell to 248. Calculate the percentage decrease. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 72 ÷ 320 = 0.225, so the percentage decrease is 22.5%, which is 23% to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Define the term biodiversity.
acceptedAnswers: variety of all the different species
variety of species in an ecosystem
markScheme: 1 mark: the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem
questions.explanation: The definition must refer to the variety of different species, not to the number of individuals.

questions.question: Give two ways in which humans depend on other species.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: food; medicines; materials such as wood or fibres; pollination of crops; clean water or fertile soil
questions.explanation: Humans rely on biodiversity for food, materials and medicines, and on ecosystem services such as pollination.

questions.question: Name two human activities that are reducing biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: deforestation; building; quarrying; farming/monocultures; dumping waste; pollution; global warming
questions.explanation: These activities destroy or change habitats, or kill organisms directly, so fewer species survive.

questions.question: Explain why an ecosystem with high biodiversity is more stable than one with low biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark: species are less dependent on one other species (for food, shelter or the physical environment)
1 mark: so if one species is lost, others can use alternative food sources or shelter and the ecosystem is not disrupted as much
questions.explanation: The key idea is reduced dependence: a predator with several prey can switch if one prey species declines.

questions.question: Explain why the future of the human species relies on maintaining a good level of biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark: humans depend on other species for food, materials or medicines
1 mark: undiscovered species may provide future medicines or foods / ecosystems provide services such as pollination or clean water; extinct species are lost for ever
questions.explanation: Our food crops, medicines and materials all come from other species, and many species have not yet been studied.

questions.question: A woodland contains many species of tree. Describe two ways the trees help to maintain the physical environment for other organisms.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: provide shelter or nesting sites; provide shade (lower temperature, higher humidity); roots hold soil together and reduce erosion; leaf litter adds nutrients and humus to soil
questions.explanation: Organisms rely on each other not only for food but for the physical conditions they live in.

questions.question: A pest is accidentally introduced to an island and kills one of only three species of tree. Suggest and explain the effects on the island's animals.
markScheme: 1 mark: animals that fed on or sheltered in that tree lose food or habitat
1 mark: with only three tree species (low biodiversity), the animals are highly dependent on each one, so their populations fall or they die out
1 mark: other effects, for example more competition for the remaining trees, or predators of those animals also decline
questions.explanation: In a low-biodiversity ecosystem the loss of one producer has knock-on effects through the food web, because there are few alternatives.

questions.question: A student says: 'A field of 10 000 maize plants has a higher biodiversity than a pond with 30 different species.' Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: biodiversity is the variety (number) of different species, not the number of individuals
1 mark: the field is (mostly) one species, while the pond has 30 species, so the pond has higher biodiversity
questions.explanation: The student has confused biodiversity with population size.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by biodiversity and explain why it is important for both ecosystems and humans.
markScheme: Indicative content: definition: variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth or within an ecosystem; importance for ecosystems: stability, reduced dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and maintenance of the physical environment; example of predator switching prey or pollinators; importance for humans: food, materials, medicines, ecosystem services such as pollination and clean water; future of humans relies on maintaining biodiversity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct definition plus clear explanation of importance for both ecosystems and humans.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a definition or simple statements of importance, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives the precise definition, then explains stability in terms of dependence, and gives specific human benefits.

questions.question:
Scientists surveyed two areas of farmland. Area A has small fields surrounded by hedgerows and a small wood. Area B is one very large field of wheat with no hedgerows. The results are shown below.
Area A: 54 plant species, 31 bird species, 120 insect species.
Area B: 6 plant species, 4 bird species, 18 insect species.
Use the data and your knowledge to compare the biodiversity of the two areas and explain why the differences are important for the stability of the ecosystems and for humans.
markScheme: Indicative content: Area A has much higher biodiversity for all groups (54 vs 6 plant species, 9 times as many; 31 vs 4 bird species; 120 vs 18 insect species); hedgerows and wood provide varied habitats, food and shelter; Area B is a monoculture with few habitats.

Stability: in A species are less dependent on one another for food and shelter; predators have alternative prey; in B a pest or disease affecting wheat or one insect would have large effects; B less stable.

Humans: A supports pollinators and natural predators of crop pests, which help food production; biodiversity provides food, medicines and materials; reduction in biodiversity is caused by human activities such as farming; future of humans relies on maintaining biodiversity.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison using data, clear explanation of stability in terms of dependence, and relevant benefits to humans.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): comparison with some data and some explanation of stability or human importance.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that A has more species, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The best answers manipulate the data (for example 54 ÷ 6 = 9 times as many plant species), link hedgerows to habitat variety, and explain stability using reduced dependence.

questions.question: State why biodiversity on Earth is falling at present.
markScheme: 1 mark: human activities (such as deforestation, pollution, land use or global warming)
questions.explanation: The AQA specification states that many human activities are reducing biodiversity.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a reason that species depend on each other in an ecosystem?
options: Food
Choosing which genes to pass on
Shelter
Maintenance of the physical environment
markScheme: 1 mark: choosing which genes to pass on
questions.explanation: Species depend on each other for food, shelter and maintenance of the physical environment. Organisms cannot choose which genes they pass on.
